item.title: Kyo-Wagashi: Kyoto's Seasonal Sweets — Guide
item.description: Kyo-wagashi are the refined traditional sweets of Kyoto, developed alongside the tea ceremony and elevated here into an edible art form. Made largely from sweet bean paste, glutinous rice, agar and sugar, they are prized less for sweetness than for beauty: each is shaped and coloured to evoke a season — a pink petal in spring, a cool cube of kingyoku in summer, a russet maple leaf in autumn. Served with a bowl of bitter matcha, a single wagashi is a small ceremony in itself.

item.title: Yoshino Kuzu: The Translucent Sweet of the Mountains — Guide
item.description: Yoshino kuzu is one of Japan’s most refined traditional ingredients: a pure white starch painstakingly extracted from the roots of wild kudzu vines and refined by hand in cold mountain water, a labour-intensive craft centred on the Yoshino region. Prized for its smooth, glossy texture, real Yoshino hon-kuzu transforms into some of the most elegant wagashi in Japan — silken, jelly-like kuzumochi dusted with kinako and syrup, translucent kuzukiri noodles dipped in kuromitsu, and, in winter, kuzuyu, a warm, soothing thickened drink.

item.title: Kyoto Cooking Class Guide: Learn Japanese Home Cooking
item.description: A cooking class is one of the most rewarding things a food-loving visitor can do in Kyoto — and one of the few souvenirs you can take home and use forever. In a few hours, a friendly local instructor teaches you to make real Japanese home cooking — washoku staples, Kyoto’s vegetable-forward obanzai, sushi, ramen, or delicate wagashi sweets — often after a guided shop through Nishiki Market to choose your ingredients.
